title: Hear, decode, and pronounce French
lessons:
# Chapter 1 — Hear, decode, and pronounce French

## What you will learn
By the end, you can connect common spellings to sounds, notice syllable rhythm, distinguish several useful vowel contrasts, and use a few polite survival phrases. No prior French is assumed. Start here even if you have studied before; if the decoding tasks feel easy, skim the sound map and move on while keeping the bank for review. This is a pronunciation foundation, not an accent test.

## A practical sound map
French spelling is more regular than English, but a written letter does not always make a separate sound. Final consonants are often silent: in `petit` (small), the final **t** is usually not pronounced. The written **-ent** ending of a third-person plural present-tense verb is silent, as in `ils parlent` (they speak); do not generalize this to every word containing those letters—`vient` (comes) has a pronounced nasal vowel. Do not pronounce every written letter. By contrast, an ending consonant may be heard before a following vowel through liaison in familiar expressions, as in `vous avez` (you have); treat liaison as connected speech, not a reason to pronounce every final consonant everywhere.

French vowels are made with a steady mouth shape. In `tu` (you), the **u** is a tight, rounded front vowel: say “ee” while rounding the lips. In `tout` (all), **ou** is like “oo.” These are different sounds. The nasal vowels in `bon` (good), `pain` (bread), and `blanc` (white) let air resonate through the nose; the written **n** is not a separate final /n/ in these examples. Accent marks help distinguish spelling and sometimes sound: `é` is a closed, pure vowel held steady—like the start of English “say,” but without the glide at the end—while `è` is more open. Learn each word with its sound rather than relying on an English spelling guess.

French rhythm groups words into short sense units. The final pronounced syllable of a group receives the main prominence; avoid giving every word an English-style stress. Link words smoothly but keep the phrase understandable. Clickable French in this lesson is wrapped in backticks for optional synthetic audio; listen, repeat once slowly, then once at ordinary pace. Browser voices vary and are not authentic exam recordings.

## First useful chunks
`Bonjour` (hello/good morning) works in many daytime encounters; `Bonsoir` (good evening) is used later in the day. `Salut` (hi/bye) is informal. Use `s'il vous plaît` (please) and `merci` (thank you) to make a request courteous. `Excusez-moi` (excuse me) can open a question or get someone's attention. A natural first repair is `Je ne comprends pas` (I don't understand), followed by `Pouvez-vous répéter ?` (Could you repeat?). Memorize the whole chunk; do not wait to understand every grammatical piece.

## Decode without panic
When a new written phrase appears, first mark vowel groups (`ou`, `oi`, `au`, `eau`, `an/en`, `on`, `in/ain`). Next, identify likely silent endings. Then listen to the phrase and imitate its rhythm. If a sound is uncertain, compare two words rather than forcing an English sound onto it. You only need intelligibility and useful listening distinctions now; perfect imitation is not a prerequisite for communication.

## Try the skills
The listening activities use short connected messages: listen for the whole situation and one key detail. Reading practice checks whether spelling clues help you understand a practical sign. For speaking, say a short greeting and repair phrase from memory before opening the model. For writing, produce a two-line message that uses a greeting and thanks. Models are examples, not the only acceptable answers.

## Cumulative retrieval
Try to answer from memory before opening each block. Then say the French aloud once.

Before the first reveal: From memory, give a daytime greeting and say thank you. Name the normally silent ending consonant in petit, then distinguish the vowels in tout and tu.

:::answer
`Bonjour` = hello / good morning. `Merci` = thank you. The **t** at the end of `petit` is normally silent. `ou` in `tout` is not the same vowel as **u** in `tu`.
:::

Before the second reveal: Ask someone politely in French to repeat, and add the French word for “please.”

:::answer
To ask someone to repeat, use `Pouvez-vous répéter ?` For a polite request, add `s'il vous plaît`. Do not pronounce every final consonant just because it is written.
:::

## Self-check and spaced review
You are ready to continue when you can (1) identify **ou** versus **u** in familiar words, (2) give the gist of a short greeting, and (3) say a polite repair phrase without reading. Record one sound you confuse. Review 12 bank items today, the same missed items tomorrow, again after three days, and once after a week. On each review, retrieve first, listen second, and only then inspect the English meaning. If the script is easy but audio is hard, repeat listening; if both are easy, progress to Chapter 2.

bank.prompt: Hear the greeting; identify its register.
Recall the greeting used in the evening.
bank.cue: It begins with bon- and suits evening.
It addresses someone formally or plurally.

bank.prompt: Use this to get someone's attention politely.

bank.cue: Listen for ne...pas around the verb.

bank.prompt: Ask a person to repeat politely.
bank.cue: A pouvoir form begins the question.

bank.fr: Parlez plus lentement, s'il vous plaît.
bank.prompt: Make a polite request for slower speech.

bank.cue: It asks how things are going.

bank.prompt: Recall a farewell meaning see you soon.
bank.cue: The first word starts with à.
The farewell is followed by a formal title.
Keep the possessive mon before livre.

bank.prompt: Listen for whether a /t/ links c'est and une.
bank.cue: This liaison is optional and often omitted in informal speech; it is not required.
The last adjective describes the door.

bank.prompt: Translate and notice the final sound in chaud.
Listen for the nasal vowel in bon.
bank.cue: Do not add a separate final n.

bank.en: I like the sound of French.
bank.prompt: Say the sentence with a smooth rhythm group.
Notice linking between tu and as, then as and un.
bank.cue: Three short vowel starts connect smoothly.

bank.prompt: Translate the sentence without pronouncing silent endings.
bank.cue: The final s in les is not a separate sound.
The place is a short word beginning with i.
It has four letters and begins n.
The adjective is plural in writing.

bank.prompt: Distinguish the vowel in rue from ou.
bank.cue: Round the lips for the tight front vowel.

bank.prompt: Translate and identify the ou sound.
bank.cue: The first word has the vowel of English 'oo'.

bank.prompt: Retrieve a phrase for a short break.
Listen for the nasal vowel in train.
bank.cue: The word rhymes approximately with pain.

bank.prompt: Use the phrase to say you are hungry.
bank.cue: French uses avoir, literally have hunger.

bank.prompt: Translate, keeping the final vowel clear.
bank.cue: The color ends in a pronounced vowel sound.

bank.prompt: Order politely with a short phrase.
Understand the temperature of the water.

bank.cue: The question word has a grave accent.

bank.en: The station is on the left.

bank.prompt: Understand the location of the exit.

bank.fr: Le musée ferme à six heures.
bank.en: The museum closes at six o'clock.
bank.cue: Listen for the number after à.

bank.prompt: Say what place you are looking for.

bank.cue: Use the formal command of aider.
A male speaker uses the written form shown.

bank.prompt: Rewrite this sentence for a female speaker.
bank.cue: Add the feminine spelling to perdu.
The final adjective begins with s.

bank.prompt: Decide whether the place is far away.
Hear the state of the window.

bank.fr: Ouvrez la porte, s'il vous plaît.

bank.en: I would like a glass of water.
bank.prompt: Order a glass of water politely.
bank.cue: The conditional voud- softens the request.

bank.prompt: Specify that you do not want sugar.

bank.fr: Avec du lait, s'il vous plaît.
bank.prompt: Translate the addition to an order.

bank.cue: The final word begins with c.
The two-word direction begins with par.
The command is addressed to vous.

bank.prompt: Identify whether the market is open.
Replace bus with rue and adjust the demonstrative to agree.
bank.cue: Use cette with the feminine noun rue.

bank.fr: La prochaine rue est à droite.
bank.en: The next street is on the right.
bank.prompt: Follow the direction in the message.
bank.cue: À droite is the final location phrase.
The command is followed by au feu.
Rouge begins with a French uvular sound.

bank.prompt: Use a modest statement about comprehension.
Tell someone which language you speak.

bank.cue: Put un peu before the language.

bank.fr: Épelez votre nom, s'il vous plaît.
La lettre est sur la table.
bank.en: The letter is on the table.
The pen falls onto the floor.
bank.cue: Par terre means onto the floor/on the ground.
The final noun is plural keys.

bank.fr: Le sac est sous la chaise.
bank.en: The bag is under the chair.

bank.fr: La chaise est près de la fenêtre.
bank.en: The chair is near the window.

bank.cue: Use the fixed phrase il y a.

bank.prompt: Translate the reassurance and time word.

bank.fr: Je suis ici pour un rendez-vous.
La clinique est au premier étage.
bank.en: The clinic is on the first floor.
The elevator is out of order.
bank.cue: En panne signals something is not working.

bank.en: Use the stairs on the right.
bank.cue: The noun is singular in French.

bank.fr: La porte du fond est ouverte.
bank.en: The door at the back is open.
bank.cue: Du fond means at the back.
A possessive formal address precedes aide.
The short reply begins with avec.

bank.prompt: Recognize a polite reply to thanks.
bank.cue: It is a fixed courteous expression.

bank.prompt: Identify why the speaker asks again.

bank.fr: Le mot commence par une voyelle.
bank.en: The word begins with a vowel.

bank.prompt: Recall how to describe an unpronounced ending.

bank.en: I'm starting again from the beginning.
bank.cue: Depuis le début means from the beginning.

activities.title: At the information desk
activities.prompt: Listen to the connected announcement and choose the place the visitor needs.
activities.script: Bonjour, madame. Je cherche la gare, s'il vous plaît. — La gare est à gauche, après la pharmacie. — Merci beaucoup !
options: The station, to the left after the pharmacy
The pharmacy, to the right of the station
The bus stop, behind the hotel
activities.explanation: The visitor asks for the station; the reply says it is on the left, after the pharmacy.

activities.title: A short service update
activities.prompt: Listen without reading a script. What should the customer do because of the problem?
activities.script: Attention, l'ascenseur est en panne aujourd'hui. Pour aller à la clinique, prenez l'escalier à droite. Le rendez-vous est au premier étage.
options: Take the stairs on the right
Return to the appointment desk tomorrow
activities.explanation: The elevator is out of order, so the announcement directs visitors to the stairs on the right.

activities.title: Read a shop notice
activities.prompt: Read the French notice and identify when the shop opens.
activities.passage: PETITE BOUTIQUE — Fermée ce matin. Ouverture à quatorze heures. Merci de votre patience.
activities.explanation: Quatorze heures is 14:00; the notice says the shop is closed this morning.

activities.title: Find a room
activities.prompt: Read the direction and identify where the meeting room is.
activities.passage: La salle de réunion est au fond du couloir, porte bleue. L'ascenseur ne fonctionne pas; prenez l'escalier à gauche.
options: At the end of the corridor, behind the blue door
Beside the elevator, behind a red door
At the start of the corridor, upstairs
Outside the building, near the stairs
activities.explanation: Au fond du couloir means at the end of the corridor; the blue door identifies the room.

activities.title: First polite encounter
activities.prompt: Imagine you have arrived at a community centre. Greet the receptionist, say your name, thank them, and ask them to repeat one direction slowly. Speak for about 20 seconds.
activities.model: Bonjour ! Je m'appelle Alex. Excusez-moi, pouvez-vous répéter plus lentement, s'il vous plaît ? Merci beaucoup.
rubric: I used a suitable greeting and gave my name.
I asked for repetition politely and clearly.
My phrases were understandable; I paused between ideas.

activities.title: A two-line message
activities.prompt: Write a short note to a French-speaking host: greet them, explain that you do not understand one direction, and politely ask them to repeat it. Aim for 20–35 words.
activities.model: Bonjour, je suis devant la gare. Je ne comprends pas bien la direction. Pouvez-vous répéter plus lentement, s'il vous plaît ? Merci beaucoup !
rubric: The note has a greeting and clear context.
It states the problem and makes a polite request.
The phrases are legible and the message is easy to follow.
